t: You got one copy of every instruction from each parent. So what happens when the two copies disagree?
Every gene you have arrives in duplicate — one from each parent. They are frequently not the same, and the cell has to do something about that.
sub: Two recipes for the same thing, and they say different things.
There is no vote and no averaging. What actually happens is stranger and simpler.

question: Your two copies say different things. What do you end up with?
The two alleles differ. What determines the outcome?
options: It depends which one still works
stages.outcome: It depends which one still works
note: Have a guess before you look.
Commit. The everyday framing of 'strong' and 'weak' genes gets this badly wrong, and the correct answer is more mechanical.

t: Put each pair of copies with what you would end up with.
Match each pair of alleles to the result.
Any answer fits any slot here, so the marking is on you. Work out each cross.
Placement is unconstrained. Predict the phenotype ratio for each cross, given that the working allele is dominant.

label: Both parents carry two working copies
Both parents carry one working and one broken copy
One parent has two broken copies, the other has one of each
Both parents carry two broken copies

name: Two carriers have a child
Carrier × carrier
pass: One in four. That is why healthy parents can have an affected child.
1 in 4 affected — the classic recessive ratio, and why two unaffected carriers can have an affected child.
fail: Not right. Each parent has one broken copy to pass on, so work out the four combinations.
Reconsider: each parent transmits one of two alleles independently, giving four equally likely combinations.

name: An affected parent and a carrier
Affected × carrier
pass: Half. The affected parent can only pass on a broken copy.
1 in 2 — the affected parent transmits a broken allele with certainty, so the outcome rests entirely on the carrier.
fail: Not right. One parent has nothing but broken copies to give.
Reconsider: a homozygote has only one allele to transmit, which collapses the cross to a single coin flip.

win: You can now predict a cross before it happens.
That is the whole of Mendelian prediction: alleles segregate independently, so the ratios follow from counting combinations.
lose: Look at which cross you missed — it says what to think about.
Read the failed trial: each names the step in the reasoning to revisit, and you can reassign and test again.

t: A copy that still works even when the other is broken is called dominant.
When one working copy is enough, that version is dominant and the broken one is recessive.
Dominance describes the relationship between alleles at a locus, not a property of either allele alone. Most recessive conditions are recessive because one functional copy makes enough product.

Dominance is a statement about the mapping from genotype to phenotype, and it is not intrinsic. The same allele can be dominant for one trait and recessive for another — sickle-cell is recessive for the anaemia and effectively dominant for malaria resistance.
sub: It is not about being stronger. It is about one copy being enough.
Nothing overpowers anything. Usually one working copy simply produces enough of the product to do the job.

This is why most loss-of-function mutations are recessive: half the normal enzyme level is generally sufficient. The exceptions — haploinsufficiency, dominant negatives — are informative precisely because they are exceptions.
The 'strong gene beats weak gene' framing is not a simplification of this, it is a different and wrong theory. It predicts blending, which is the thing Mendel's ratios ruled out.

q: Why is a dominant copy dominant?
Why is a dominant allele dominant?
What is the usual mechanistic basis of dominance?
options: Because one working copy makes enough
Because it is stronger than the other one
Because it comes from the father
why: Nothing is fighting anything. If one copy makes enough of what you need, having a broken second copy does not show.

It is a dosage fact, not a contest. One functional allele generally produces sufficient product, so the broken one is invisible — which also explains why some conditions are not recessive: where half the normal amount is not enough, one broken copy does show.

Dominance is a consequence of the shape of the dose-response curve. Most enzymes operate well above the level at which output limits flux, so halving them changes nothing measurable. Where flux is dose-sensitive you get haploinsufficiency instead, and the same class of mutation becomes dominant.

t: This is how a doctor can tell parents the chance of passing something on.

Genetic counselling is this arithmetic applied carefully. Two carriers of a cystic fibrosis allele face a one-in-four risk in each pregnancy — independently each time, which is the part people find hardest, because three unaffected children change the fourth pregnancy's odds not at all.
